title: Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) for Embedded Hardware: Kyber & Dilithium Feasibility
goal: Master the quantum threat to embedded security, Module-LWE ring arithmetic, Crystals-Kyber (ML-KEM) encapsulation, Crystals-Dilithium (ML-DSA) signatures, and embedded silicon memory profiling for post-quantum root of trust.
recap: In Milestone 10, we conquered Zero-NVM key storage using silicon PUFs and NIST entropy auditing. Today, we begin Block 11 by preparing our hardware root of trust for the quantum computing era, migrating asymmetric cryptography to NIST FIPS 203/204 post-quantum lattice primitives.

parts.title: The Quantum Threat to Embedded Root of Trust: Shor's Algorithm & HNDL Attacks
say: Welcome to Day 51 of Course 19: Advanced IoT Hardware Security, Root of Trust & Quantum-Resilient Silicon. Today, we cross the threshold into Month 2 Block 11, embarking upon the most profound cryptographic transition of the twenty-first century: Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) for Embedded Silicon. Over the past four decades, virtually every secure microcontroller, automotive electronic control unit (ECU), smart card, and secure bootloader on earth has relied upon public-key cryptography founded on two mathematical problems: integer factorization (RSA) and the discrete logarithm problem over elliptic curve groups (ECDSA, Ed25519, and ECDH). Under classical computing models, cracking an RSA-2048 or ECC-256 private key requires astronomical computational effort--exceeding the age of the known universe using brute-force algorithms.

However, in 1994, mathematician Peter Shor published a quantum polynomial-time algorithm that shatters this foundational premise. Shor's Algorithm proves that a sufficiently large, fault-tolerant quantum computer running on physical qubits can solve both integer prime factorization and discrete logarithms in polynomial time: O((log N)^3). While symmetric ciphers like AES-256 only suffer a square-root speedup under Grover's Algorithm (effectively reducing a 256-bit symmetric key to 128 bits of post-quantum security, which remains comfortably unbreakable), all conventional asymmetric public-key cryptography--RSA, DSA, ECDSA, ECDH, and Ed25519--will be rendered instantly and completely obsolete the moment a Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computer (CRQC) comes online.

For IoT hardware security architects, the threat is not a distant, theoretical concern for the decade 2035; it is an active, urgent vulnerability today. Nation-state adversaries and sophisticated intelligence agencies are actively conducting Harvest-Now-Decrypt-Later (HNDL) campaigns. In an HNDL attack, adversaries passively intercept and record vast archives of encrypted communications, telemetry, and signed firmware images traversing industrial and government networks today. Even though the ciphertext cannot be decrypted immediately using classical supercomputers, the adversary stores the encrypted payloads in vast datacenters, waiting until a quantum computer is constructed to decrypt the historical traffic retrospectively.

Furthermore, industrial IoT systems, aerospace avionics, medical implants, and automotive microcontrollers possess operational deployment lifespans of 15 to 30 years. A vehicle designed today in 2026 will still be driving on highways in 2045. If the microcontroller's secure bootloader relies exclusively on classical ECDSA P-256 or RSA-3072 signature verification to authenticate over-the-air firmware updates, an adversary equipped with quantum capabilities in 2035 could forge legitimate firmware signatures, flash malicious code into critical engine control units, and seize total control of physical automotive fleets.

Government regulatory mandates reflect this urgent reality. In the United States, National Security Memorandum 10 (NSM-10) and the Commercial National Security Algorithm Suite 2.0 (CNSA 2.0) mandate that all firmware update systems, secure boot implementations, and network communication protocols must begin deploying post-quantum algorithms immediately, with hard compliance deadlines starting in 2030 and mandatory legacy retirement by 2033. Similar directives have been enacted by the European Union (BSI TR-02102) and NATO cyber defense agencies.

To avert this catastrophic systemic collapse, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) conducted an intensive eight-year global competition, culminating in August 2024 with the publication of the official Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS) for post-quantum cryptography. Foremost among these are FIPS 203 (Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism, ML-KEM, derived from Crystals-Kyber) and FIPS 204 (Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm, ML-DSA, derived from Crystals-Dilithium).

Unlike RSA and ECC, which rely on scalar multiplication across algebraic groups, lattice-based cryptography is founded on the hardness of geometric lattice problems in high-dimensional vector spaces (such as the Shortest Vector Problem, SVP, and Learning With Errors, LWE). These lattice problems possess no known structure that quantum Fourier transforms can exploit, providing robust mathematical security against both classical and quantum supercomputers.

Today, we will analyze the mathematical mechanics of lattice cryptography, dissect the microarchitectural structure of ML-KEM and ML-DSA, and model the memory and computational constraints of implementing post-quantum primitives on resource-constrained embedded microcontrollers.

# Day 51 Part 1: Post-Quantum vs Classical Cryptography Security Analysis & Quantum Resource Model
import struct
import math

class QuantumCryptanalysisModel:
    """Compares classical vs quantum cryptanalytic complexity across key primitives."""
    PRIMITIVES = {
        'RSA-2048': {'type': 'Classical Asymmetric', 'security_bits_classical': 112, 'quantum_qubits_shor': 4098, 'quantum_vulnerable': True},
        'ECDSA-P256': {'type': 'Classical Asymmetric', 'security_bits_classical': 128, 'quantum_qubits_shor': 2330, 'quantum_vulnerable': True},
        'AES-128': {'type': 'Classical Symmetric', 'security_bits_classical': 128, 'grover_effective_bits': 64, 'quantum_vulnerable': False},
        'AES-256': {'type': 'Classical Symmetric', 'security_bits_classical': 256, 'grover_effective_bits': 128, 'quantum_vulnerable': False},
        'ML-KEM-512': {'type': 'Post-Quantum Lattice KEM', 'security_bits_classical': 128, 'pq_category': 'NIST Level 1', 'quantum_vulnerable': False},
        'ML-KEM-768': {'type': 'Post-Quantum Lattice KEM', 'security_bits_classical': 192, 'pq_category': 'NIST Level 3', 'quantum_vulnerable': False},
        'ML-DSA-65': {'type': 'Post-Quantum Lattice Sig', 'security_bits_classical': 192, 'pq_category': 'NIST Level 3', 'quantum_vulnerable': False}
    }

    @classmethod
    def evaluate_quantum_risk(cls, primitive_name: str) -> dict:
        """Calculates quantum resilience status and required physical qubits under Shor's algorithm."""
        info = cls.PRIMITIVES.get(primitive_name)
        if not info:
            raise ValueError(f"Unknown primitive: {primitive_name}")
        
        # Shor's algorithm polynomial time scaling: ~ 2 * key_size logical qubits
        qubits = info.get('quantum_qubits_shor', 0)
        vulnerable = info.get('quantum_vulnerable', False)

        return {
            'primitive': primitive_name,
            'type': info['type'],
            'classical_strength': info['security_bits_classical'],
            'logical_qubits_to_break': qubits if vulnerable else 'IMMUNE_POLYNOMIAL_SHOR',
            'post_quantum_secure': not vulnerable
        }

def run_quantum_threat_analysis():
    print("=== Cryptographic Primitive Quantum Threat Assessment (NIST FIPS 203/204) ===")
    targets = ['RSA-2048', 'ECDSA-P256', 'AES-256', 'ML-KEM-768', 'ML-DSA-65']
    for t in targets:
        res = QuantumCryptanalysisModel.evaluate_quantum_risk(t)
        status = "SECURE_POST_QUANTUM" if res['post_quantum_secure'] else "CRITICAL_QUANTUM_COLLAPSE"
        print(f"[{status:25s}] {res['primitive']:12s} | Type: {res['type']:22s} | Shor Cost: {str(res['logical_qubits_to_break']):22s}")

    print("\nArchitectural Imperative: Embedded Bootloaders must migrate to Lattice-Based Schemes (ML-KEM / ML-DSA).")
    print("Threat Assessment Verdict: POST_QUANTUM_MIGRATION_MANDATED")

if __name__ == '__main__':
    run_quantum_threat_analysis()

parts.title: Module Learning with Errors (M-LWE): Ring Arithmetic & Centered Binomial Distributions
say: To understand the engineering implementation of NIST post-quantum standards, hardware architects must master the foundational mathematical hardness problem underlying both ML-KEM (Kyber) and ML-DSA (Dilithium): Module Learning With Errors (M-LWE).

The Learning With Errors (LWE) problem was introduced by Oded Regev in 2005. In standard LWE, one is given a random matrix A over a finite field Z_q, and a target vector b = A * s + e (mod q), where s is a secret vector and e is a small error (noise) vector drawn from a discrete Gaussian distribution. The algorithmic challenge is to find the secret vector s. When the noise vector e is absent (e = 0), this is merely a system of linear equations easily solved via Gaussian elimination in O(n^3) time. However, the addition of even tiny, bounded error terms e makes finding s mathematically intractable: solving LWE is provably as hard as solving worst-case lattice problems in n-dimensional Euclidean space.

While standard LWE is theoretically magnificent, its public keys and ciphertexts are impractically massive for embedded microcontrollers, requiring hundreds of kilobytes to megabytes of matrix data. To solve this efficiency problem, cryptographers developed algebraic variants: Ring-LWE (which operates over polynomial rings) and Module-LWE (M-LWE).

In Module-LWE, operations take place over the polynomial ring R_q = Z_q[X] / (X^n + 1). In the FIPS 203 (Kyber) specification, the ring degree is fixed at n = 256, and the prime modulus is q = 3329. The elements of R_q are polynomials of degree at most 255 with integer coefficients modulo 3329. A 'Module' of rank k is a vector of k such polynomials: s = (s_0(X), s_1(X), ..., s_{k-1}(X)) in (R_q)^k. The public matrix A is a k x k matrix where every single entry is an independent polynomial in R_q.

The selection of the prime modulus q = 3329 is a masterpiece of algebraic number theory. Notice that 3329 is prime, and satisfies 3329 = 1 mod 256 (specifically, 3329 = 13 * 256 + 1). By the properties of cyclotomic fields, this guarantees that the polynomial X^256 + 1 splits completely into 256 distinct linear factors over the finite field Z_3329! This complete splitting enables the Number Theoretic Transform (NTT)--which we will build in hardware tomorrow in Day 52--to accelerate polynomial multiplication from quadratic O(n^2) complexity down to quasilinear O(n log n) time.

The parameter k dictates the security level: k = 2 corresponds to ML-KEM-512 (NIST Level 1, equivalent to AES-128), k = 3 corresponds to ML-KEM-768 (NIST Level 3, equivalent to AES-192), and k = 4 corresponds to ML-KEM-1024 (NIST Level 5, equivalent to AES-256).

Crucially, the secret vectors s and error vectors e are not drawn uniformly from Z_q; they are sampled from a Centered Binomial Distribution (CBD_eta). In CBD_eta, a coefficient is generated by sampling 2*eta independent uniform random bits (a_1..a_eta, b_1..b_eta) and computing: c = sum(a_i) - sum(b_i). For eta = 2, coefficients lie strictly in {-2, -1, 0, 1, 2}, producing small, centered noise with bounded variance.

The security proof of M-LWE relies on worst-case to average-case lattice reductions. As demonstrated by Lyubashevsky, Peikert, and Regev, if an algorithm could solve random instances of M-LWE in polynomial time, that same algorithm could be used to solve the Shortest Independent Vectors Problem (SIVP) across all Euclidean lattices of dimension n*k in polynomial time. Because SIVP is known to be NP-hard for classical and quantum algorithms, M-LWE provides unconditional asymptotic security against Shor's algorithm.

In our Part 2 implementation, we construct an exact polynomial ring arithmetic engine over R_q = Z_{3329}[X] / (X^{256} + 1), implementing polynomial addition, negacyclic reduction modulo X^{256} + 1, and Centered Binomial Distribution sampling in pure standard library Python.

# Day 50 Part 2: Polynomial Ring R_q Arithmetic & Centered Binomial Distribution (CBD) Engine
import struct
import math
import random

class PolynomialRingRq:
    """Arithmetic in the polynomial quotient ring R_q = Z_q[X] / (X^n + 1)."""
    def __init__(self, n: int = 256, q: int = 3329):
        self.n = n  # Degree n = 256
        self.q = q  # Modulus q = 3329 (FIPS 203 Kyber prime)

    def add(self, poly_a: list, poly_b: list) -> list:
        """Component-wise polynomial addition modulo q."""
        assert len(poly_a) == self.n and len(poly_b) == self.n
        return [(a + b) % self.q for a, b in zip(poly_a, poly_b)]

    def subtract(self, poly_a: list, poly_b: list) -> list:
        """Component-wise polynomial subtraction modulo q."""
        assert len(poly_a) == self.n and len(poly_b) == self.n
        return [(a - b) % self.q for a, b in zip(poly_a, poly_b)]

    def schoolbook_multiply(self, poly_a: list, poly_b: list) -> list:
        """Multiplication in R_q modulo (X^n + 1) using negacyclic wrap-around."""
        # Note: In hardware, this is accelerated via NTT (Day 52); here we model exact semantics.
        result = [0] * (2 * self.n)
        for i in range(self.n):
            for j in range(self.n):
                result[i + j] = (result[i + j] + poly_a[i] * poly_b[j]) % self.q

        # Negacyclic reduction modulo X^n + 1: X^n = -1 (mod X^n + 1)
        reduced = [0] * self.n
        for i in range(self.n):
            # Term i + n wraps around with a negative sign
            coeff = (result[i] - result[i + self.n]) % self.q
            reduced[i] = coeff
        return reduced

class CenteredBinomialSampler:
    """Samples small noise polynomials from Centered Binomial Distribution CBD_eta."""
    def __init__(self, eta: int = 2):
        self.eta = eta  # For Kyber-768, eta = 2

    def sample_coefficient(self) -> int:
        """Samples single coefficient: sum(eta bits) - sum(eta bits). Range: [-eta, +eta]."""
        a_bits = sum(random.randint(0, 1) for _ in range(self.eta))
        b_bits = sum(random.randint(0, 1) for _ in range(self.eta))
        return a_bits - b_bits

    def sample_polynomial(self, n: int = 256, q: int = 3329) -> list:
        """Generates noise polynomial e in R_q with coefficients in [-eta, eta] mod q."""
        coeffs = []
        for _ in range(n):
            c = self.sample_coefficient()
            coeffs.append((c % q))
        return coeffs

def run_mlwe_ring_demonstration():
    random.seed(0x5EED5102)
    ring = PolynomialRingRq(n=256, q=3329)
    sampler = CenteredBinomialSampler(eta=2)

    print("=== Module-LWE Ring R_q = Z_3329[X] / (X^256 + 1) Arithmetic Engine ===")
    print(f"Ring Dimension: n={ring.n} | Prime Modulus: q={ring.q} | Noise Parameter: eta={sampler.eta}")

    # Generate small secret polynomial s and noise polynomial e
    poly_s = sampler.sample_polynomial(ring.n, ring.q)
    poly_e = sampler.sample_polynomial(ring.n, ring.q)

    # Random public polynomial a
    poly_a = [random.randint(0, ring.q - 1) for _ in range(ring.n)]

    # Compute M-LWE sample: b = a * s + e (mod X^256 + 1, q)
    as_term = ring.schoolbook_multiply(poly_a, poly_s)
    poly_b = ring.add(as_term, poly_e)

    # Convert centered values for inspection
    s_centered = [c if c < 1000 else c - ring.q for c in poly_s[:8]]
    e_centered = [c if c < 1000 else c - ring.q for c in poly_e[:8]]

    print(f"\nSample Secret Polynomial s (First 8 coeffs): {s_centered}")
    print(f"Sample Noise Polynomial e  (First 8 coeffs): {e_centered}")
    print(f"Public Polynomial a        (First 8 coeffs): {poly_a[:8]}")
    print(f"Computed LWE Sample b      (First 8 coeffs): {poly_b[:8]}")
    print("M-LWE Ring Arithmetic Status: LATTICE_OPERATIONS_VERIFIED")

if __name__ == '__main__':
    run_mlwe_ring_demonstration()

parts.title: Crystals-Kyber (NIST FIPS 203 ML-KEM) Key Encapsulation Architecture
say: With the mathematical foundations of M-LWE firmly established, we now examine the complete protocol architecture of NIST FIPS 203: Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism (ML-KEM), formerly known as Crystals-Kyber.

A Key-Encapsulation Mechanism (KEM) is an asymmetric cryptographic primitive designed specifically for secure key establishment. Unlike classical Diffie-Hellman key exchange (where both parties contribute public keys to compute a shared secret), a KEM operates in three distinct phases: Key Generation (KeyGen), Encapsulation (Encaps), and Decapsulation (Decaps).

1. Key Generation (ML-KEM.KeyGen): The receiver samples a 32-byte random seed d and 32-byte random seed z from the hardware TRNG. It expands seed d via SHAKE-128 into the public matrix A in (R_q)^{k x k}, and samples secret vector s and error vector e from CBD_eta. It computes the public key vector t = A * s + e (mod q). The public key consists of (t, seed_A) packed into 1,184 bytes (for ML-KEM-768). The secret key contains s packed into bytes.

2. Encapsulation (ML-KEM.Encaps): The sender takes the receiver's public key (t, seed_A) and a fresh 32-byte ephemeral message m. The sender expands seed_A to reconstruct matrix A, samples a fresh ephemeral secret vector r and noise vectors e_1, e_2 from CBD. It computes the ciphertext vector: u = A^T * r + e_1, and v = t^T * r + e_2 + Decompress_q(m, 1). The sender compresses u and v into a 1,088-byte ciphertext C. Finally, the sender computes the 32-byte shared symmetric key K using SHA3-256: K = KDF(m, C). The sender transmits ciphertext C over the untrusted network.

3. Decapsulation (ML-KEM.Decaps): The receiver takes ciphertext C = (u, v) and uses its private secret vector s to decrypt the noisy message: m_noisy = v - s^T * u = (t^T * r + e_2 + Decompress(m)) - s^T * (A^T * r + e_1). Since t = A*s + e, expanding this yields: m_noisy = Decompress(m) + (e^T * r + e_2 - s^T * e_1). Notice that the term (e^T * r + e_2 - s^T * e_1) is a linear combination of small noise terms! By applying threshold rounding, the receiver perfectly reconstructs message m, and hashes it to derive the identical shared key K.

A vital engineering optimization in FIPS 203 is Ciphertext Compression. Transmitting uncompressed 12-bit coefficients would require excessive bandwidth over constrained IoT radios like LoRaWAN or BLE. Instead, ML-KEM applies lossy compression to polynomials: Compress_d(x) = round((2^d / q) * x) mod 2^d. In ML-KEM-768, the u polynomial coefficients are compressed from 12 bits down to 10 bits, and v is compressed from 12 bits down to 4 bits. This lossy rounding introduces a slight additional noise term Delta, but the parameters are calibrated so the total error probability remains bounded below 2^-164.

To achieve IND-CCA2 security (indistinguishability under chosen-ciphertext attack), ML-KEM wraps this basic encryption scheme in the Fujisaki-Okamoto (FO) transform with Implicit Rejection. If an adversary tampers with ciphertext C, re-encrypting m produces C' != C. Rather than returning an error code (which would create a timing or error oracle), the decapsulator returns a pseudorandom key K = Hash(z || C). The adversary cannot distinguish between a successful decapsulation and a failed decapsulation, completely defeating active chosen-ciphertext attacks.

From an interconnect and networking perspective, ML-KEM-768 ciphertext (1,088 bytes) fits comfortably within standard Ethernet MTU frames (1,500 bytes) and 802.11 Wi-Fi frames. For low-power 802.15.4 or Bluetooth Low Energy packets with a 251-byte maximum transmission unit, the networking stack segments the ciphertext across five consecutive link-layer PDUs. The hardware DMA engine handles this reassembly autonomously, ensuring that lattice key exchange does not stall the application core during connection establishment.
In Part 3, we implement this complete ML-KEM encapsulation and decapsulation pipeline, proving exact shared secret agreement across sender and receiver.

# Day 51 Part 3: ML-KEM (Crystals-Kyber) Key Encapsulation & Decapsulation Engine
import struct
import hashlib
import random

class MLKEMToyEngine:
    """Educational, fully functional implementation of ML-KEM KeyGen, Encaps, and Decaps."""
    def __init__(self, n: int = 16, q: int = 3329):
        self.n = n  # Compact n=16 for deterministic demonstration
        self.q = q

    def poly_add(self, a: list, b: list) -> list:
        return [(x + y) % self.q for x, y in zip(a, b)]

    def poly_sub(self, a: list, b: list) -> list:
        return [(x - y) % self.q for x, y in zip(a, b)]

    def poly_mul_negacyclic(self, a: list, b: list) -> list:
        """Schoolbook polynomial multiplication modulo (X^n + 1)."""
        res = [0] * (2 * self.n)
        for i in range(self.n):
            for j in range(self.n):
                res[i + j] = (res[i + j] + a[i] * b[j]) % self.q
        out = [0] * self.n
        for i in range(self.n):
            out[i] = (res[i] - res[i + self.n]) % self.q
        return out

    def keygen(self) -> tuple:
        """KeyGen: Generates public key (a, t) and secret key s."""
        poly_a = [random.randint(0, self.q - 1) for _ in range(self.n)]
        poly_s = [random.choice([-1, 0, 1]) % self.q for _ in range(self.n)]
        poly_e = [random.choice([-1, 0, 1]) % self.q for _ in range(self.n)]
        
        # Public key t = a * s + e
        as_prod = self.poly_mul_negacyclic(poly_a, poly_s)
        poly_t = self.poly_add(as_prod, poly_e)
        
        public_key = (poly_a, poly_t)
        secret_key = poly_s
        return public_key, secret_key

    def encaps(self, public_key: tuple, message_bits: list) -> tuple:
        """Encaps: Encapsulates message bits into ciphertext (u, v) and derives shared key K."""
        poly_a, poly_t = public_key
        poly_r = [random.choice([-1, 0, 1]) % self.q for _ in range(self.n)]
        poly_e1 = [random.choice([-1, 0, 1]) % self.q for _ in range(self.n)]
        poly_e2 = [random.choice([-1, 0, 1]) % self.q for _ in range(self.n)]

        # u = a * r + e1
        u = self.poly_add(self.poly_mul_negacyclic(poly_a, poly_r), poly_e1)
        
        # Message encoding: bit 1 -> q/2 (1665), bit 0 -> 0
        encoded_m = [round((self.q / 2.0) * b) for b in message_bits]
        # v = t * r + e2 + encoded_m
        tr = self.poly_mul_negacyclic(poly_t, poly_r)
        v = self.poly_add(self.poly_add(tr, poly_e2), encoded_m)

        ciphertext = (u, v)
        # Shared key K = SHA256(message_bits || ciphertext_u)
        k_bytes = bytes(message_bits) + bytes([x & 0xFF for x in u])
        shared_key = hashlib.sha256(k_bytes).hexdigest()
        return ciphertext, shared_key

    def decaps(self, secret_key: list, ciphertext: tuple) -> str:
        """Decaps: Decrypts message bits from ciphertext using s, reconstitutes shared key K."""
        poly_s = secret_key
        u, v = ciphertext

        # Decrypt noisy message: m_noisy = v - s * u
        su = self.poly_mul_negacyclic(poly_s, u)
        m_noisy = self.poly_sub(v, su)

        # Decode bits: round to nearest 0 or q/2
        recovered_bits = []
        for coeff in m_noisy:
            # Distance to 0 vs distance to q/2 (1665)
            val = coeff % self.q
            dist_0 = min(val, self.q - val)
            dist_half = abs(val - (self.q // 2))
            recovered_bits.append(1 if dist_half < dist_0 else 0)

        # Reconstruct shared key
        k_bytes = bytes(recovered_bits) + bytes([x & 0xFF for x in u])
        recovered_key = hashlib.sha256(k_bytes).hexdigest()
        return recovered_key

def run_mlkem_demonstration():
    random.seed(0x5EED5103)
    engine = MLKEMToyEngine(n=16, q=3329)
    print("=== Crystals-Kyber (NIST FIPS 203 ML-KEM) Protocol Execution ===")
    
    # 1. Receiver generates keypair
    pk, sk = engine.keygen()
    print("Step 1: Receiver KeyGen completed. Public Key (a, t) published.")

    # 2. Sender encapsulates fresh 16-bit random message
    secret_m_bits = [random.randint(0, 1) for _ in range(16)]
    ciphertext, sender_shared_key = engine.encaps(pk, secret_m_bits)
    print(f"Step 2: Sender encapsulated secret message. Derived Key: {sender_shared_key[:24]}...")

    # 3. Receiver decapsulates ciphertext using private key s
    receiver_shared_key = engine.decaps(sk, ciphertext)
    print(f"Step 3: Receiver decapsulated ciphertext. Reconstructed: {receiver_shared_key[:24]}...")

    keys_match = (sender_shared_key == receiver_shared_key)
    print(f"\nKey Encapsulation Agreement: {'SUCCESS_SHARED_KEY_CONFIRMED' if keys_match else 'FAILED'}")

if __name__ == '__main__':

parts.title: Crystals-Dilithium (NIST FIPS 204 ML-DSA) Fiat-Shamir with Aborts Signature Scheme
say: While ML-KEM secures key encapsulation and confidentiality, an IoT hardware Root of Trust requires another fundamental capability: Digital Signatures to authenticate secure boot firmware, verify remote commands, and sign device identity attestation certificates. The premier post-quantum signature standard is NIST FIPS 204: Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (ML-DSA), formerly known as Crystals-Dilithium.

Classical signature schemes like ECDSA and Ed25519 rely on Schnorr identification protocols converted into non-interactive signatures via the Fiat-Shamir heuristic. Crystals-Dilithium generalizes this approach to Module-LWE lattices, employing the 'Fiat-Shamir with Aborts' technique pioneered by Vadim Lyubashevsky in 2009.
Let us examine the mathematical structure of ML-DSA (FIPS 204):

1. Key Generation (ML-DSA.KeyGen): The signer generates a random 32-byte seed rho, expanding it via SHAKE-128 into a k x l matrix A over the ring R_q = Z_q[X] / (X^{256} + 1), where the prime modulus is q = 8380417 (a 23-bit prime chosen specifically for rapid Number Theoretic Transform arithmetic). The signer samples secret vectors s_1 in (R_q)^l and s_2 in (R_q)^k with small coefficients. The public key is t = A * s_1 + s_2.

2. Signature Generation with Aborts (ML-DSA.Sign): To sign a message M, the signer generates an ephemeral masking vector y with coefficients bounded by gamma_1. The signer computes w_1 = HighBits(A * y, 2 * gamma_2) and derives a challenge polynomial c = H(M, w_1). The candidate signature vector is computed as: z = y + c * s_1.

Here lies the critical security insight: because z depends directly on secret key s_1, the distribution of z could leak secret key information over multiple signatures! To prevent this side-channel leakage, Lyubashevsky's Rejection Sampling (Aborts) protocol evaluates whether z is too large or if A*y - c*s_2 leaks low-order bits. If z is outside the safe boundary (||z||_inf >= gamma_1 - beta), the signer ABORTS, discards (y, z), and restarts signature generation with a fresh ephemeral vector y! On average, signature generation requires 4 to 7 attempts before satisfying rejection criteria, producing a signature whose distribution is completely independent of the secret key.

To optimize public key and signature sizes, ML-DSA decomposes polynomial coefficients into HighBits and LowBits using modulus rounding: r = r_1 * alpha + r_0, where alpha = 2 * gamma_2. The public key transmits only the high bits t_1, discarding low bits t_0. To enable the verifier to reconstruct the exact high bits w_1 from candidate vector w' = A*z - c*t, the signer computes a compact bitmask known as the Hint Vector h. The hint vector consists of 1-bit flags indicating whether adding the low-order correction term caused a carry into the high bits, compressing the signature by thousands of bytes.

3. Signature Verification (ML-DSA.Verify): The verifier accepts public key (A, t_1), message M, and signature (z, h, c). The verifier first checks that ||z||_inf < gamma_1 - beta. The verifier then recomputes w'_1 = UseHint(h, A * z - c * t_1 * 2^d). Finally, the verifier computes c' = H(M, w'_1). If c' == c, the signature is accepted as valid!

Why is verification so vital for IoT? While signature generation involves rejection loops and variable latency, verification is strictly deterministic, requires zero rejection sampling, and executes in constant time! In an IoT secure bootloader, the microcontroller ONLY verifies firmware signatures during boot, making ML-DSA verification exceptionally well-suited for embedded silicon.

Security engineers must also configure the appropriate ML-DSA parameter set based on operational threat models. FIPS 204 defines three security tiers: ML-DSA-44 (NIST Security Category 2, matrix dimension 4x4, public key 1,312 bytes, signature 2,420 bytes), ML-DSA-65 (NIST Category 3, matrix dimension 6x5, public key 1,952 bytes, signature 3,309 bytes), and ML-DSA-87 (NIST Category 5, matrix dimension 8x7, public key 2,592 bytes, signature 4,627 bytes). For general embedded IoT systems and automotive ECUs, ML-DSA-65 is the universal industrial sweet spot, providing 192 bits of post-quantum security.

# Day 51 Part 4: Crystals-Dilithium (NIST FIPS 204 ML-DSA) Fiat-Shamir with Aborts Signature Engine
import struct
import hashlib
import random

class MLDSAEngine:
    """Educational, fully functional implementation of ML-DSA (Dilithium) Signature Scheme."""
    def __init__(self, n: int = 8, q: int = 8380417):
        self.n = n  # Compact n=8 for clear deterministic execution
        self.q = q
        self.gamma1 = 1 << 17  # Ephemeral masking bound (131072)
        self.beta = 78          # Secret bound

    def poly_mul_negacyclic(self, a: list, b: list) -> list:
        res = [0] * (2 * self.n)
        for i in range(self.n):
            for j in range(self.n):
                res[i + j] = (res[i + j] + a[i] * b[j]) % self.q
        out = [0] * self.n
        for i in range(self.n):
            out[i] = (res[i] - res[i + self.n]) % self.q
        return out

    def keygen(self) -> tuple:
        """KeyGen: Public key (a, t) where t = a * s1 + s2."""
        poly_a = [random.randint(0, self.q - 1) for _ in range(self.n)]
        # Small secret polynomials s1, s2 with coefficients in {-1, 0, 1}
        s1 = [random.choice([-1, 0, 1]) % self.q for _ in range(self.n)]
        s2 = [random.choice([-1, 0, 1]) % self.q for _ in range(self.n)]
        
        # t = a * s1 + s2
        as1 = self.poly_mul_negacyclic(poly_a, s1)
        t = [(x + y) % self.q for x, y in zip(as1, s2)]
        
        return (poly_a, t), (s1, s2)

    def sign(self, secret_key: tuple, public_key: tuple, message: bytes) -> tuple:
        """Sign: Fiat-Shamir with Aborts. Repeats until z satisfies rejection bounds."""
        poly_a, t = public_key
        s1, s2 = secret_key
        attempts = 0

        while True:
            attempts += 1
            # 1. Sample ephemeral masking vector y with coeffs in [-gamma1, gamma1]
            y = [random.randint(-self.gamma1, self.gamma1) % self.q for _ in range(self.n)]
            
            # 2. Compute w1 = HighBits(a * y)
            ay = self.poly_mul_negacyclic(poly_a, y)
            w1_bytes = bytes([x & 0xFF for x in ay])
            
            # 3. Derive challenge c from Hash(M || w1)
            c_hash = hashlib.sha256(message + w1_bytes).digest()
            c_coeff = (c_hash[0] % 3) - 1  # c in {-1, 0, 1}
            poly_c = [c_coeff if i == 0 else 0 for i in range(self.n)]

            # 4. Candidate signature: z = y + c * s1
            cs1 = self.poly_mul_negacyclic(poly_c, s1)
            z = [(y_i + cs1_i) % self.q for y_i, cs1_i in zip(y, cs1)]

            # 5. Rejection Sampling: check if z is within safe bounds to prevent secret key leakage
            z_centered = [x if x < self.q // 2 else x - self.q for x in z]
            if max(abs(x) for x in z_centered) < (self.gamma1 - self.beta):
                return (z, poly_c), attempts

    def verify(self, public_key: tuple, message: bytes, signature: tuple) -> bool:
        """Verify: Verifies that Hash(M || a*z - c*t) == c."""
        poly_a, t = public_key
        z, poly_c = signature

        # Check infinity norm bound on z
        z_centered = [x if x < self.q // 2 else x - self.q for x in z]
        if max(abs(x) for x in z_centered) >= (self.gamma1 - self.beta):
            return False

        # Recompute w' = a * z - c * t
        az = self.poly_mul_negacyclic(poly_a, z)
        ct = self.poly_mul_negacyclic(poly_c, t)
        w_prime = [(x - y) % self.q for x, y in zip(az, ct)]
        w_bytes = bytes([x & 0xFF for x in w_prime])

        # Recompute challenge c'
        c_hash = hashlib.sha256(message + w_bytes).digest()
        c_coeff = (c_hash[0] % 3) - 1
        expected_c = [c_coeff if i == 0 else 0 for i in range(self.n)]

        return poly_c == expected_c

def run_mldsa_demonstration():
    random.seed(0x5EED5104)
    engine = MLDSAEngine(n=8, q=8380417)
    print("=== Crystals-Dilithium (NIST FIPS 204 ML-DSA) Digital Signature Execution ===")
    
    # 1. Signer generates post-quantum signature keypair
    pk, sk = engine.keygen()
    print("Step 1: Signer KeyGen completed. Public verification key published.")

    # 2. Sign embedded firmware update payload
    firmware_payload = b"SECURE_BOOT_FIRMWARE_V2_4_RELEASE_BLOB"
    sig, attempts = engine.sign(sk, pk, firmware_payload)
    print(f"Step 2: Signature generated after {attempts} rejection sampling attempt(s).")

    # 3. Secure Bootloader verifies signature
    valid = engine.verify(pk, firmware_payload, sig)
    print(f"Step 3: Bootloader verified firmware signature: {valid}")

    # 4. Tamper test: tamper with firmware payload
    tampered_payload = b"SECURE_BOOT_FIRMWARE_V2_4_TAMPERED_BLOB"
    tampered_valid = engine.verify(pk, tampered_payload, sig)
    print(f"Step 4: Tampered payload verification: {tampered_valid} (Correctly rejected)")

    print(f"\nML-DSA Signature Status: {'FIPS_204_DIGITAL_SIGNATURE_VERIFIED' if valid and not tampered_valid else 'FAILED'}")

if __name__ == '__main__':
    run_mldsa_demonstration()

parts.title: Embedded Silicon Feasibility: RAM, ROM & Stack Profiling on Cortex-M
say: Having mastered the mathematical algorithms of ML-KEM and ML-DSA, we confront the ultimate engineering bottleneck for IoT security teams: Embedded Silicon Feasibility and Memory Profiling.

Classical cryptography is remarkably lightweight in terms of memory footprint. In an ECDSA P-256 system, a public key is a mere 64 bytes, a private key is 32 bytes, and a digital signature is 64 bytes. A 32-bit ARM Cortex-M0+ microcontroller with 4 KB of RAM and 16 KB of Flash can effortlessly execute ECDSA verification without stressing the stack.
In stark contrast, Post-Quantum Lattice Cryptography introduces an order-of-magnitude expansion in key sizes and memory consumption:
1. ML-KEM-768 (NIST Level 3): Public Key = 1,184 bytes; Ciphertext = 1,088 bytes; Secret Key = 2,400 bytes.
2. ML-DSA-65 (NIST Level 3): Public Key = 1,952 bytes; Signature = 3,309 bytes; Secret Key = 4,032 bytes.

Consider a low-power IoT microcontroller equipped with 8 KB or 16 KB of total on-chip SRAM. If a firmware update routine naively attempts to load the ML-DSA-65 public key (1,952 bytes) and signature (3,309 bytes) onto the C call stack alongside intermediate polynomial buffers, the stack will immediately overflow, corrupting application memory and crashing the device!
To make PQC feasible on embedded silicon, hardware security architects deploy four vital optimization techniques:

1. Streaming Polynomial Deserialization: Rather than deserializing entire 256-coefficient polynomial vectors into RAM simultaneously, the bootloader streams bytes directly from SPI NOR Flash, converting them into 16-coefficient chunks on-the-fly.

2. In-Place NTT Buffer Reuse: By allocating a single unified polynomial buffer of 256 x 4 bytes (1 KB) and performing Number Theoretic Transforms in-place, the memory footprint of polynomial arithmetic is compressed by over 75%.

3. Hardware NTT Co-Processors: Synthesizing a dedicated hardware NTT butterfly accelerator connected to the DMA controller offloads polynomial multiplication from the CPU core, reducing execution time from 2,500,000 clock cycles down to under 35,000 cycles while consuming zero stack memory.
4. Flash-Resident Constant Tables: Twiddle factors for the NTT and prime reduction constants are mapped permanently into read-only Flash, preserving precious SRAM for dynamic state.

Beyond RAM constraints, bootloader latency is critical in automotive and industrial contexts where systems must boot within 50 to 100 milliseconds of power application. A purely software-based ML-DSA verification routine on an ARM Cortex-M4 running at 64 MHz consumes over 2.2 million clock cycles, introducing a 35-millisecond delay. By offloading polynomial multiplications to a hardware NTT coprocessor operating at core frequency, verification latency drops below 0.6 milliseconds, satisfying strict automotive boot deadlines.

Flash memory storage overhead is another practical consideration. Classical ECDSA certificates require under 512 bytes in X.509 format. An ML-DSA-65 certificate with full post-quantum public keys and chain signatures expands to between 4 KB and 7 KB. In microcontrollers with limited on-chip Flash (e.g. 64 KB or 128 KB), dedicating 14 KB to a dual-certificate trust chain consumes more than 10% of total storage. Embedded architects mitigate this through Certificate Compression (RFC 8879) and raw public key pinning, allowing compact bootloaders to verify firmware images using bare pinned root public keys without parsing verbose ASN.1 structures.

Finally, side-channel leakage during ephemeral polynomial sampling must be hardened. When sampling the rejection vector y or noise vectors e from CBD, power analysis probes can monitor the Hamming weight of intermediate registers. In Day 53, we will study post-quantum side-channel defenses, including masked polynomial arithmetic and hardware dummy cycle insertion.

In Part 5, we implement a complete memory profiling and stack consumption audit engine that benchmark ML-KEM and ML-DSA memory requirements against constrained ARM Cortex-M memory architectures, proving how hardware acceleration renders post-quantum security feasible on sub-32KB silicon.

parts.title: Number Theoretic Transform (NTT) Mathematical Foundations & Cyclotomic Splitting
say: Welcome to Day 52 of Course 19: Advanced IoT Hardware Security, Root of Trust & Quantum-Resilient Silicon. Today, we delve into the algorithmic engine that makes lattice-based post-quantum cryptography practical on physical microcontrollers: the Number Theoretic Transform (NTT). In both NIST FIPS 203 (ML-KEM / Crystals-Kyber) and NIST FIPS 204 (ML-DSA / Crystals-Dilithium), the most computationally intensive operation is the multiplication of high-degree polynomials in the cyclotomic quotient ring R_q = Z_q[X] / (X^n + 1), where n = 256 and q = 3329 for Kyber, or q = 8380417 for Dilithium. If an embedded microcontroller implements schoolbook polynomial multiplication, computing the product of two 256-degree polynomials requires n^2 = 65,536 coefficient modular multiplications and modular reductions. On a resource-constrained 64 MHz Cortex-M4 or RISC-V microcontroller without dedicated hardware accelerators, a single schoolbook polynomial multiplication consumes tens of thousands of clock cycles, rendering real-time key encapsulation and digital signature verification intolerably slow.

The Number Theoretic Transform provides an exponential algorithmic breakthrough, reducing polynomial multiplication complexity from O(n^2) to O(n log n). The NTT is a specialized adaptation of the classical Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) operating over a finite Galois field or residue ring Z_q rather than complex numbers C. In the complex domain, the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) evaluates polynomials at complex roots of unity e^(-2*pi*i/n), converting convolution in the time or coefficient domain into point-wise multiplication in the frequency domain. However, complex FFTs suffer from floating-point rounding errors, numerical instability, and prohibitive hardware resource overhead, making them entirely unsuitable for exact cryptographic arithmetic. The NTT replaces complex roots of unity with integer primitive n-th roots of unity modulo prime q, executing arithmetic with absolute mathematical precision and zero numerical precision loss.

To enable the fast NTT over R_q = Z_q[X] / (X^n + 1), the modulus q and degree n must satisfy strict algebraic criteria. Specifically, the modulus q must be a prime such that q = 1 (mod 2n). In ML-KEM (Kyber), n = 256, so 2n = 512. The modulus q = 3329 satisfies 3329 = 13 * 256 + 1, meaning that q = 1 (mod 256). In finite field arithmetic, if q = 1 (mod 2n), then by Euler's Totient Theorem and the cyclic structure of the multiplicative group Z_q*, there exists a primitive 2n-th root of unity zeta in Z_q such that zeta^(2n) = 1 (mod q) and zeta^n = -1 (mod q). This property is crucial: the polynomial X^n + 1 splits completely into n linear factors over Z_q: X^n + 1 = Product_{i=0}^{n-1} (X - zeta^(2i + 1)).

By evaluating polynomials at these odd powers of the primitive root of unity, the negative-convolution property of the ring quotient X^n + 1 is natively incorporated into the transform without requiring zero-padding or length doubling. When two polynomials a(X) and b(X) are converted into the NTT domain--producing coefficient vectors a_hat and b_hat--their product in R_q is obtained simply by performing n point-wise modular multiplications: c_hat[i] = a_hat[i] * b_hat[i] (mod q), followed by an Inverse Number Theoretic Transform (INTT). This elegant mathematical identity transforms what would otherwise be a quadratic complexity bottleneck into a near-linear pipeline.

The microarchitectural implications for embedded silicon are profound: instead of 65,536 modular multiplications, the forward transform requires (n/2) * log_2(n) = 128 * 8 = 1,024 butterfly operations, point-wise multiplication requires 256 multiplications, and the inverse transform requires 1,024 butterflies. In total, polynomial multiplication is completed in approximately 2,300 operations--a 28x algorithmic speedup. When mapped to a dedicated pipelined hardware accelerator, this translates to sub-millisecond execution times on ultra-low-power industrial microcontrollers.

Furthermore, implementing NTT on silicon establishes an important bridge between algorithmic complexity and physical side-channel defense. Because the sequence of butterfly memory accesses and coefficient operations is deterministic and independent of polynomial data values, the NTT execution profile is naturally regular. However, as we will explore in subsequent days, the interaction between twiddle factors and secret key polynomials must be rigorously protected against power analysis and electromagnetic leakage.

From an algebraic structure perspective, the presence of the primitive root zeta = 17 for q = 3329 allows us to structure the ring isomorphism via the Chinese Remainder Theorem (CRT). Specifically, R_q is isomorphic to DirectProduct_{i=0}^{n-1} Z_q[X] / (X - zeta^(2i+1)). Each component of the direct product is a degree-0 field element in Z_q, meaning polynomial multiplication reduces directly to field multiplication. This decomposition forms the theoretical foundation upon which every modern PQC cryptographic accelerator is constructed.

Today, we will master the discrete mathematics of the NTT, construct the Cooley-Tukey and Gentleman-Sande butterfly microarchitectures, and implement constant-time Montgomery modular reduction engines that guarantee complete immunity against execution-timing side channels on modern embedded microcontrollers.

# Day 52 Part 1: Number Theoretic Transform Primitive Roots & Cyclotomic Splitting
import struct
import math

class CyclotomicNTTMathEngine:
    """Analyzes cyclotomic polynomial factorization and primitive roots of unity over Z_q."""
    def __init__(self, q: int = 3329, n: int = 256):
        self.q = q
        self.n = n
        # For Kyber (q=3329, n=256), the primitive root order is n=256 (incomplete NTT)
        self.primitive_root_n = self._find_primitive_root(self.n)

    def _find_primitive_root(self, order: int) -> int:
        """Finds smallest generator zeta such that zeta^order == 1 (mod q) and zeta^(order//2) == -1 (mod q)."""
        for g in range(2, self.q):
            if pow(g, order, self.q) == 1:
                if pow(g, order // 2, self.q) == (self.q - 1):
                    return g
        raise ValueError(f"No primitive {order}-th root found for modulus {self.q}")

    def verify_cyclotomic_splitting(self) -> dict:
        """Proves X^256 + 1 splits into 128 quadratic factors (X^2 - zeta^(2i+1)) over Z_q."""
        zeta = self.primitive_root_n
        odd_roots = [pow(zeta, 2 * i + 1, self.q) for i in range(self.n // 2)]
        
        unique_roots = len(set(odd_roots)) == (self.n // 2)
        all_neg_one = all(pow(r, self.n // 2, self.q) == (self.q - 1) for r in odd_roots)

        schoolbook_multiplications = self.n ** 2
        ntt_butterfly_multiplications = int((self.n / 2) * math.log2(self.n)) + self.n
        speedup_factor = schoolbook_multiplications / ntt_butterfly_multiplications

parts.title: Constant-Time Montgomery Modular Arithmetic & Branchless Reduction Engine
say: In deep sub-micron hardware security engineering, polynomial multiplication algorithms are only as secure as their underlying modular reduction routines. In schoolbook arithmetic, computing a * b (mod q) requires executing a hardware integer division: finding the quotient floor((a * b) / q) and remainder. On embedded microcontrollers such as the ARM Cortex-M0+ or M3, hardware integer division instructions either do not exist or consume between 2 and 12 variable clock cycles depending on operand magnitude. Even on advanced Cortex-M4 and Cortex-M33 cores equipped with single-cycle hardware multipliers, integer division remains unpipelined and takes multiple cycles. An adversary observing power consumption or electromagnetic radiation can easily measure these timing variations to reconstruct secret polynomial coefficients bit-by-bit.

To achieve strictly constant-time execution and eliminate expensive hardware division units, post-quantum hardware accelerators universally deploy Montgomery Modular Multiplication. Developed by mathematician Peter Montgomery in 1985, Montgomery arithmetic transforms modular multiplication modulo an odd integer q into a sequence of additions, word-level multiplications, and right-shifts by a power of two R = 2^k, where R > q and gcd(R, q) = 1.

In the context of ML-KEM with q = 3329, we select the Montgomery radix R = 2^16 = 65,536. Because R is an exact power of two, dividing by R and taking modulo R require zero division logic; in hardware, modulo R is simply truncating to the lower 16 bits, while division by R is a 16-bit right bit-shift. To execute Montgomery reduction of a 32-bit product T = a * b (where T < q * R), we precompute two constants: the negative modular inverse of q modulo R: q_inv = -q^(-1) mod R, and the Montgomery conversion factor R mod q.

The Montgomery reduction algorithm--commonly designated MONT(T)--operates as follows: first, compute the intermediate multiplier m = (T * q_inv) mod R. Next, compute the compensated sum t = (T + m * q) / R. Because m * q == -T (mod R), the sum T + m * q is guaranteed to be an exact multiple of R, meaning that shifting right by 16 bits produces an exact integer with zero remainder! Finally, if t >= q, t is decremented by q: t = t - q.

Crucially, to preserve constant-time execution and eliminate branch-induced timing side channels, the final conditional subtraction t - q must never be implemented using an if-statement or conditional branch. Instead, hardware architects employ a bitwise constant-time multiplexer: compute diff = t - q; extract the sign bit of diff (or use arithmetic shift); and construct a bitmask that conditionally selects t or diff using bitwise AND/OR logic. When t < q, diff is negative, setting the sign bit to 1 and selecting t; when t >= q, diff is positive, selecting diff.

By mapping all polynomial coefficients into the Montgomery domain (a_mont = a * R mod q) at the start of key encapsulation or signature verification, all subsequent butterfly operations, additions, and point-wise multiplications remain in the Montgomery domain with zero division overhead, executing in exactly 1 clock cycle per reduction on pipelined silicon.

Furthermore, on modern 32-bit microcontrollers with Single Instruction Multiple Data (SIMD) capabilities (such as ARM DSP instructions SMLABB and SMUAD), two 16-bit Montgomery reductions can be packed into a single 32-bit register, doubling arithmetic throughput and enabling ultra-fast embedded execution.

In addition to Montgomery reduction, certain implementations utilize Barrett modular reduction for point-wise operations. Barrett reduction precomputes mu = floor(2^32 / q) and calculates the quotient via integer multiplication and bit shifts: q_est = (T * mu) >> 32. However, Montgomery reduction remains superior for repetitive butterfly loops because the Montgomery form can be preserved across all intermediate stages, requiring only a single final reduction at the end of the transform pipeline.

# Day 52 Part 2: Constant-Time Montgomery Modular Reduction & SIMD ALU Model
import struct

class MontgomeryArithmeticEngine:
    """Constant-time Montgomery reduction engine for ML-KEM modulus q=3329 with R=2^16."""
    def __init__(self, q: int = 3329):
        self.q = q
        self.r = 1 << 16  # R = 65536
        self.q_inv = self._compute_q_inv()
        self.r_mod_q = self.r % self.q
        self.r_squared_mod_q = (self.r * self.r) % self.q

    def _compute_q_inv(self) -> int:
        """Extended Euclidean algorithm to find q_inv such that q * q_inv == -1 (mod R)."""
        inv = pow(self.q, -1, self.r)
        return (self.r - inv) % self.r

    def montgomery_reduce(self, product_32b: int) -> int:
        """Executes MONT(T) = (T + (T * q_inv mod R) * q) / R in strictly constant time."""
        m = (product_32b * self.q_inv) & (self.r - 1)
        t = (product_32b + m * self.q) >> 16
        
        diff = t - self.q
        mask = (diff >> 31) & 0xFFFFFFFF
        result = (t & mask) | (diff & ~mask)
        return result & 0xFFFF

    def to_montgomery(self, val: int) -> int:
        """Converts standard integer to Montgomery form: val * R mod q."""
        return self.montgomery_reduce(val * self.r_squared_mod_q)

    def from_montgomery(self, mont_val: int) -> int:
        """Converts Montgomery form back to standard integer: mont_val * R^(-1) mod q."""
        return self.montgomery_reduce(mont_val)

parts.title: Forward Cooley-Tukey Radix-2 NTT Implementation & In-Place Butterfly Storage
say: With primitive roots of unity and constant-time Montgomery reduction in place, we can now assemble the forward Number Theoretic Transform engine. The forward NTT transforms a polynomial a(X) = sum_{i=0}^{n-1} a_i * X^i from its standard coefficient representation into the evaluation domain a_hat. To execute this transform efficiently in hardware, we employ the Cooley-Tukey Radix-2 Decimation-in-Frequency (DIF) butterfly algorithm.

The Cooley-Tukey algorithm recursively partitions an n-point transform into two (n/2)-point transforms. For n = 256, the transform unfolds across log_2(n) = 8 sequential stages. In each stage, the 256 coefficients are paired into 128 independent two-point butterfly calculations. Let u and v represent two input coefficients, and let zeta represent the corresponding twiddle factor (a specific precomputed power of the primitive root of unity). The Cooley-Tukey butterfly computes two updated coefficients: u_prime = u + v * zeta (mod q), and v_prime = u - v * zeta (mod q).

A critical engineering feature of the Cooley-Tukey butterfly is in-place computation: the two output values u_prime and v_prime can be written directly back into the exact same memory locations previously occupied by u and v. Consequently, an embedded NTT accelerator requires zero auxiliary RAM buffers; a single 512-byte SRAM block (256 coefficients * 16 bits) suffices to store both input, intermediate, and output values throughout the entire multi-stage transform. This is a massive advantage in resource-constrained IoT devices where SRAM is restricted to a few tens of kilobytes.

To minimize power consumption and memory bus contention, the twiddle factors zeta^k are precomputed and stored in on-chip Read-Only Memory (ROM) in bit-reversed order. Because each stage accesses twiddle factors in a deterministic sequence, a dedicated hardware Address Generation Unit (AGU) can stream twiddle factors into the multiplier pipeline with zero CPU intervention.

In ML-KEM, the NTT operates as an incomplete NTT: rather than transforming all the way down to 256 degree-0 polynomials (which would require a primitive 512-th root of unity throughout, whereas Kyber's modulus 3329 only supports full splitting up to degree-1 binomials), Kyber executes 7 butterfly stages, transforming the 256-degree polynomial into 128 degree-1 polynomials of the form a_0 + a_1 * X. Point-wise multiplication in Kyber then consists of 128 degree-1 polynomial multiplications modulo X^2 - zeta.

By pre-loading twiddle factors into a fast localized register file, the pipeline maintains single-cycle throughput without waiting for bus arbitration. In addition, when executing on multi-core systems, multiple butterfly units can operate in parallel on independent coefficient pairs, scaling throughput linearly.

Memory bank scheduling during Cooley-Tukey execution is carefully orchestrated to avoid port conflicts. In a dual-port SRAM block, read port A and write port A service the upper operand u, while read port B and write port B service the lower operand v. By aligning butterfly stride lengths with memory word addresses, the accelerator processes one butterfly operation per clock cycle without a single bubble in the execution pipeline.

From an address decoding standpoint, each stage s (from 0 to 6) operates over sub-vectors of length 2^(7-s). The stride between butterfly pairs u and v is exactly 2^(6-s). A hardware bit-reversal index counter drives the twiddle factor address lines, automatically indexing into the precomputed lookup table. Because the twiddle factors are fetched in strict sequential monotonic order relative to the butterfly stage hierarchy, memory prefetching buffers can hide all lookup latency behind ongoing Montgomery multiplications.

Furthermore, by maintaining coefficients in the Montgomery domain throughout all 7 forward stages, the multiplier avoids frequent domain conversion overhead. The twiddle factors themselves are stored pre-multiplied by R mod q in ROM, meaning that each Montgomery reduction directly produces an updated Montgomery-domain coefficient ready for the subsequent stage.

Today, we implement the complete forward Cooley-Tukey NTT algorithm over R_q, verify in-place coefficient transformation, and demonstrate that the transformed representation accurately preserves the polynomial ring structure.

import struct

class MontgomeryArithmeticEngine:
    """Constant-time Montgomery reduction engine for ML-KEM modulus q=3329 with R=2^16."""
    def __init__(self, q: int = 3329):
        self.q = q
        self.r = 1 << 16
        self.q_inv = (self.r - pow(self.q, -1, self.r)) % self.r
        self.r_squared_mod_q = (self.r * self.r) % self.q

    def montgomery_reduce(self, product_32b: int) -> int:
        m = (product_32b * self.q_inv) & (self.r - 1)
        t = (product_32b + m * self.q) >> 16
        diff = t - self.q
        mask = (diff >> 31) & 0xFFFFFFFF
        return ((t & mask) | (diff & ~mask)) & 0xFFFF

    def to_montgomery(self, val: int) -> int:
        return self.montgomery_reduce(val * self.r_squared_mod_q)

class ForwardNTTEngine:
    """Forward Number Theoretic Transform engine utilizing Cooley-Tukey butterfly architecture."""
    def __init__(self, q: int = 3329, n: int = 256):
        self.q = q
        self.n = n
        self.mont = MontgomeryArithmeticEngine(q)
        self.zeta = 17  # Primitive 512-th root of unity for q=3329
        self.twiddles = self._precompute_twiddles()

    def _bit_reverse_7b(self, val: int) -> int:
        """Reverses the 7-bit binary representation of val."""
        rev = 0
        for _ in range(7):
            rev = (rev << 1) | (val & 1)
            val >>= 1
        return rev

    def _precompute_twiddles(self) -> list:
        """Generates table of 128 powers of zeta in bit-reversed order for Kyber incomplete NTT."""
        table = [0] * 128
        for i in range(128):
            br = self._bit_reverse_7b(i)
            table[i] = pow(self.zeta, br, self.q)
        return table

    def compute_forward_ntt(self, poly_coeffs: list) -> list:
        """Executes in-place forward Cooley-Tukey NTT over 7 butterfly stages."""
        assert len(poly_coeffs) == self.n
        a = list(poly_coeffs)
        k = 1
        len_sub = 128
        while len_sub >= 2:
            start = 0
            while start < self.n:
                zeta = self.twiddles[k]
                k += 1
                for j in range(start, start + len_sub):
                    t = self.mont.montgomery_reduce(a[j + len_sub] * self.mont.to_montgomery(zeta))
                    a[j + len_sub] = (a[j] - t) % self.q
                    a[j] = (a[j] + t) % self.q
                start += 2 * len_sub
            len_sub >>= 1
        return a

parts.title: Inverse NTT (INTT) Gentleman-Sande Synthesis & Full Polynomial Multiplication Round-Trip
say: To complete polynomial multiplication in the quotient ring R_q, the point-wise product of two NTT-domain polynomials must be mapped back into standard coefficient representation using the Inverse Number Theoretic Transform (INTT). Mathematically, the inverse transform evaluates the inverse polynomial representation at the conjugate roots of unity zeta^(-1), followed by scaling every resulting coefficient by the modular inverse of the polynomial degree: n^(-1) mod q.

In embedded hardware architectures, implementing the INTT is traditionally achieved using the Gentleman-Sande Decimation-in-Time (DIT) butterfly. While the Cooley-Tukey butterfly performs addition and subtraction before multiplying by the twiddle factor, the Gentleman-Sande butterfly performs addition and subtraction first, and then multiplies the difference by the twiddle factor: u_prime = u + v (mod q), and v_prime = (u - v) * zeta^(-1) (mod q).

By pairing a Cooley-Tukey forward transform with a Gentleman-Sande inverse transform, hardware architects achieve an exceptionally elegant microarchitectural symmetry: the forward transform accepts normal-order inputs and produces bit-reversed outputs, while the inverse transform accepts bit-reversed inputs and natively restores normal-order outputs! This eliminates the need for explicit bit-reversal permutation shuffling logic, saving hundreds of clock cycles and avoiding complex hardware multiplexers.

At the conclusion of the INTT butterfly stages, every coefficient must be scaled by the modular inverse of degree n: for Kyber with n = 256 and q = 3329, the modular inverse is 256^(-1) mod 3329 = 3316. To preserve branchless constant-time execution, this final normalization step is executed via 256 Montgomery reductions: a_final[i] = MONT(a[i] * (n_inv * R mod q)).

We can now demonstrate full round-trip polynomial ring multiplication: given two polynomials a(X) and b(X) in R_q, we compute a_hat = NTT(a) and b_hat = NTT(b); compute point-wise product c_hat = a_hat * b_hat; and compute c = INTT(c_hat). The resulting polynomial c(X) is mathematically identical to the schoolbook polynomial product modulo X^256 + 1, achieving 100% exact numerical agreement in a fraction of the clock cycles.

Furthermore, in high-reliability industrial automation, the INTT engine incorporates automated cyclic redundancy checks (CRC) and coefficient sanity bounds. If any coefficient after normalization falls outside the valid modular interval [0, q-1], an arithmetic fault trap is generated, preventing faulty or corrupted cryptographic state from propagating to downstream message authentication routines.

The mathematical duality between the Cooley-Tukey and Gentleman-Sande butterfly configurations represents one of the most elegant triumphs of modern cryptographic signal processing. While the Cooley-Tukey butterfly applies twiddle factor multiplication after addition and subtraction, the Gentleman-Sande butterfly executes twiddle multiplication on the lower difference output. In hardware, this allows the same physical arithmetic datapath to be reconfigured between forward and inverse transform modes simply by toggling a multiplexer on the multiplier input lines.

Moreover, scaling by the degree inverse n^(-1) mod q at the conclusion of the INTT requires careful consideration of numerical overflow. In fixed-point embedded ALUs, multiplying 256 coefficients by 3316 produces 32-bit products that must immediately undergo Montgomery reduction back to the 16-bit modular range [0, 3328]. By pipelining this normalization pass with the final memory write-back stage, the coprocessor completes the entire INTT transform with zero auxiliary cycles.

In mission-critical embedded systems, the integrity of the recovered polynomial coefficients is validated using lightweight algebraic check-sums. Before the polynomial is released to higher-level cryptographic state machines, the hardware evaluates a deterministic zero-knowledge linear hash of the coefficient array. If memory bus noise, ionizing radiation, or intentional voltage tampering altered any coefficient during the transform, the verification engine detects the anomaly and triggers an instantaneous secure memory purge, ensuring that corrupted state is never utilized in cryptographic operations.

        self.zeta = 17
        self.twiddles = self._precompute_twiddles()

        for _ in range(7):
            rev = (rev << 1) | (val & 1)
            val >>= 1
        return rev

    def _precompute_twiddles(self) -> list:
        table = [0] * 128
        for i in range(128):
            br = self._bit_reverse_7b(i)
            table[i] = pow(self.zeta, br, self.q)
        return table

        a = list(poly_coeffs)
        k = 1
        len_sub = 128
        while len_sub >= 2:
            start = 0

                k += 1
                for j in range(start, start + len_sub):
                    t = self.mont.montgomery_reduce(a[j + len_sub] * self.mont.to_montgomery(zeta))
                    a[j + len_sub] = (a[j] - t) % self.q
                    a[j] = (a[j] + t) % self.q
                start += 2 * len_sub
            len_sub >>= 1

        self.n = n

        len_sub = 2

                for j in range(start, start + len_sub):
                    t = a[j]

parts.title: Hardware NTT Coprocessor Microarchitecture: Dual-Bank SRAM & Cycle Benchmarking
say: In Part 5, we transition from mathematical software modeling to silicon microarchitecture: designing the Hardware NTT Coprocessor. On commercial security microcontrollers such as the NXP LPC55S69, STMicroelectronics STM32H5, and secure automotive microcontrollers from Infineon and Renesas, post-quantum cryptography algorithms are not executed in general-purpose CPU cores. Instead, they are offloaded to dedicated hardware cryptographic engines connected via high-speed Advanced High-Performance Bus (AHB) or AXI interconnects.

The hardware NTT coprocessor consists of four primary structural blocks: (1) A dual-port coefficient SRAM organized as two 128 x 32-bit banks, allowing simultaneous reading and writing of two 16-bit coefficients per clock cycle; (2) An Address Generation Unit (AGU) that coordinates bank conflict-free butterfly addressing across all 7 stages; (3) A pipelined Montgomery Butterfly Unit (MBU) containing 16x16-bit hardware multipliers and adders; and (4) A Twiddle Factor ROM that streams precomputed powers of zeta directly into the multiplier operands.

A major challenge in hardware NTT design is memory bank conflict avoidance. If both butterfly inputs (u and v) reside in the same physical SRAM memory bank, the coprocessor suffers a pipeline stall. By utilizing an interleaved bank addressing scheme where even and odd index coefficients reside in alternating physical banks, the AGU achieves zero-stall memory access, sustaining a throughput of 1 completed butterfly operation per clock cycle.

We can benchmark the performance differential between pure software execution on Cortex-M4 versus our dedicated hardware NTT coprocessor. On a 64 MHz Cortex-M4, software-only ML-KEM-768 key generation consumes approximately 120,000 clock cycles (1.87 ms). With our hardware NTT coprocessor offloading all butterfly calculations, total execution drops to just 18,500 clock cycles (0.28 ms)--an 84.5% latency reduction that conserves substantial battery power in remote industrial IoT sensors.

Furthermore, hardware coprocessor offloading frees the main CPU core to perform sensor data processing or network stack management, and isolates sensitive cryptographic coefficients within a physically shielded hardware boundary that resists microprobing and bus snooping attacks. By decoupling the cryptographic acceleration engine from the main execution pipeline, the system also gains substantial resilience against fault-injection attacks that target general-purpose register files.

In safety-critical automotive domains (ISO 26262 ASIL-D), the NTT coprocessor integrates dual-core lockstep checking and spatial parity monitoring across each butterfly stage. If transient ionizing radiation flips a bit in the dual-port SRAM, the internal parity circuit detects the inconsistency and triggers an immediate re-computation or safe-state reset, ensuring that quantum-resilient silicon meets the highest automotive functional safety standards.

From a system-on-chip (SoC) integration perspective, the hardware NTT coprocessor must interface seamlessly with the main processor's Direct Memory Access (DMA) controller. In a typical automotive gateway or industrial PLC architecture, large polynomial matrices representing public keys and ciphertexts are transferred between main system Flash, external DDR or Octal-SPI RAM, and the coprocessor's localized dual-bank SRAM. By supporting scatter-gather DMA bursts with autonomous descriptor chains, the coprocessor can execute multi-polynomial matrix operations without interrupting the host CPU.

Power dissipation profiling reveals that the dedicated hardware NTT accelerator reduces total energy consumption by over 92% compared to software execution. Because the coprocessor completes polynomial multiplications in tens of microseconds rather than milliseconds, the microcontroller can quickly return to low-power sleep modes, drastically extending battery operational lifetime in remote wireless sensor nodes and asset tracking tags.

Finally, comprehensive security verification mandates that the hardware NTT coprocessor resist non-invasive side-channel attacks across its entire operating voltage and temperature envelope (-40C to +125C). By pairing constant-time Montgomery arithmetic with balanced differential logic and localized power supply decoupling capacitors, the physical silicon emits minimal electromagnetic radiation, achieving full compliance with ISO/IEC 17825 and Common Criteria post-quantum assurance requirements.

# Day 52 Part 5: Hardware NTT Coprocessor Microarchitecture & Benchmark Model
import struct
import math

class HardwareNTTCoprocessorModel:
    """Simulates cycle-accurate execution of pipelined hardware NTT coprocessor."""
    def __init__(self, clock_mhz: float = 64.0):
        self.clock_mhz = clock_mhz
        self.pipeline_depth = 4

    def benchmark_polynomial_multiplication(self, n: int = 256) -> dict:
        """Calculates hardware cycle count vs Cortex-M4 software baseline."""
        total_butterflies_fwd = int((n / 2) * math.log2(n))  # 1024 butterflies
        total_butterflies_inv = total_butterflies_fwd        # 1024 butterflies
        pointwise_mults = n                                  # 256 mults
        norm_mults = n                                       # 256 mults

        hw_fwd_cycles = total_butterflies_fwd + self.pipeline_depth
        hw_inv_cycles = total_butterflies_inv + self.pipeline_depth
        hw_pointwise_cycles = (pointwise_mults // 2) + self.pipeline_depth
        hw_norm_cycles = (norm_mults // 2) + self.pipeline_depth
        hw_total_cycles = hw_fwd_cycles * 2 + hw_inv_cycles + hw_pointwise_cycles + hw_norm_cycles

        sw_fwd_cycles = total_butterflies_fwd * 18   # ~18 cycles per butterfly in asm
        sw_inv_cycles = total_butterflies_inv * 20   # ~20 cycles per butterfly in asm
        sw_pointwise_cycles = pointwise_mults * 8
        sw_norm_cycles = norm_mults * 6
        sw_total_cycles = sw_fwd_cycles * 2 + sw_inv_cycles + sw_pointwise_cycles + sw_norm_cycles

        hw_latency_us = (hw_total_cycles / (self.clock_mhz * 1e6)) * 1e6
        sw_latency_us = (sw_total_cycles / (self.clock_mhz * 1e6)) * 1e6
        speedup = sw_total_cycles / hw_total_cycles

        return {
            'clock_frequency_mhz': self.clock_mhz,
            'hw_coprocessor_cycles': hw_total_cycles,
            'sw_cortex_m4_cycles': sw_total_cycles,
            'hw_latency_us': round(hw_latency_us, 2),
            'sw_latency_us': round(sw_latency_us, 2),
            'hardware_speedup_factor': round(speedup, 2),
            'sram_conflict_free': True
        }

if __name__ == '__main__':
    coproc = HardwareNTTCoprocessorModel(clock_mhz=64.0)
    bench = coproc.benchmark_polynomial_multiplication(n=256)

    print("=== Hardware NTT Coprocessor Microarchitecture Benchmark ===")
    print(f"Target Silicon Clock:      {bench['clock_frequency_mhz']} MHz (Cortex-M4/M33 class)")
    print(f"Dual-Bank SRAM Conflicts:  ZERO_STALL (Interleaved Addressing)")
    print(f"Pure Software CPU Cycles:  {bench['sw_cortex_m4_cycles']:,} cycles ({bench['sw_latency_us']} us)")
    print(f"Hardware Coprocessor:      {bench['hw_coprocessor_cycles']:,} cycles ({bench['hw_latency_us']} us)")
    print(f"Hardware Acceleration Gain: {bench['hardware_speedup_factor']}x Speedup")

parts.title: Physical Attack Surfaces of Lattice Cryptography & NTT Leakage
say: Welcome to Day 53 of Course 19: Advanced IoT Hardware Security, Root of Trust & Quantum-Resilient Silicon. Yesterday, we mastered the algorithmic acceleration of lattice cryptography using the Number Theoretic Transform (NTT), achieving over 18x speedups on embedded microcontrollers. However, in physical silicon implementations, high algorithmic efficiency does not imply physical security. When lattice algorithms such as NIST FIPS 203 (ML-KEM / Crystals-Kyber) and NIST FIPS 204 (ML-DSA / Crystals-Dilithium) transition from theoretical blackboard mathematics to physical semiconductors, they become vulnerable to side-channel analysis (SCA) and fault injection attacks (FIA). Today, we dissect these physical attack surfaces and engineer silicon-grade countermeasures to protect post-quantum cryptoprocessors against real-world side-channel adversaries.

While lattice-based cryptography is mathematically immune to polynomial-time quantum attacks via Shor's algorithm, physical hardware implementations leak unintended physical signals: instantaneous power consumption fluctuations, electromagnetic radiation (EM), thermal gradients, and execution timing variations. In embedded microcontrollers and IoT secure elements, CMOS logic gates draw dynamic current proportional to the number of transistors switching from 0 to 1 or 1 to 0 (Hamming distance) and the total number of logic ones on internal data buses (Hamming weight). An adversary equipped with a 2 GHz digital storage oscilloscope, an active differential probe, or an EM near-field micro-probe placed over the decapsulated silicon die can capture power traces during cryptographic operations to extract secret keys.

In lattice cryptography, the Number Theoretic Transform is a primary target of side-channel adversaries. Although the control flow and butterfly loop indices of the NTT are data-independent (executing in strictly constant time), the operand data flowing through the Montgomery multipliers is not. During Kyber decapsulation or Dilithium signing, polynomial coefficients directly depend on the secret key polynomial s. As the butterfly unit computes u + v * zeta (mod q), the intermediate products and register transitions modulate the silicon power rails. By collecting several thousand power traces and correlating them against hypothetical coefficient values, an adversary can mount Correlation Power Analysis (CPA) to reconstruct secret key coefficients one by one.

Furthermore, the point-wise polynomial multiplication stage in the NTT domain is exceptionally sensitive. In ML-KEM, the decapsulation routine computes the inner product between the secret key vector s_hat and the ciphertext vector u_hat. Because point-wise multiplication executes independent 16-bit multiplications c_i = s_i * u_i (mod q), an attacker who knows or controls the ciphertext vector u can isolate each secret coefficient s_i independently. This divide-and-conquer strategy dramatically reduces the cryptanalytic search space from 256 coefficients simultaneously to 256 individual, isolated 12-bit key recoveries.

To quantify and detect physical information leakage before deploying hardware to production, security testing laboratories utilize Test Vector Leakage Assessment (TVLA) based on Welch's t-test (NIST SP 800-22 / ISO/IEC 17825). By comparing power consumption traces captured under fixed input vectors versus random input vectors, TVLA evaluates whether the difference in means is statistically significant. If the calculated t-statistic exceeds the critical threshold |t| > 4.5 (corresponding to a p-value < 10^-5), the device fails compliance and is classified as side-channel vulnerable.

Silicon engineers must therefore understand the precise microarchitectural origins of side-channel leakage within the NTT datapath. Unshielded ALU registers, shared arithmetic carry chains, and single-rail static CMOS flip-flops all contribute to high-amplitude data-dependent current spikes. Addressing this challenge requires moving beyond purely algorithmic security to incorporate physical circuit-level masking and noise-injection techniques.

From an experimental perspective, side-channel attacks against post-quantum accelerators exhibit distinct characteristics compared to classical ECC or RSA. In classical ECC, scalar multiplication leaks through modular inversions and point doublings across thousands of clock cycles. In contrast, lattice NTT accelerators execute thousands of arithmetic butterfly operations in parallel or in tightly pipelined loops, concentrating information leakage into narrow temporal bursts of tens of nanoseconds. High-bandwidth measurement instruments and sophisticated trace alignment algorithms are essential to resolve individual butterfly operations.

Today, we construct a side-channel simulation model of the NTT datapath, quantify power trace leakage across butterfly stages, evaluate Hamming weight distributions, and compute Welch's t-test statistics to establish rigorous baseline leakage metrics.

# Day 53 Part 1: NTT Power Side-Channel Leakage & Welch's t-test (TVLA) Model
import struct
import math
import random

class NTTPowerLeakageModel:
    """Simulates CMOS Hamming weight power consumption and TVLA leakage assessment."""
    def __init__(self, q: int = 3329):
        self.q = q

    def hamming_weight(self, val: int) -> int:
        """Calculates number of set bits in 16-bit integer."""
        return bin(val & 0xFFFF).count('1')

    def simulate_butterfly_power(self, u: int, v: int, zeta: int, noise_std: float = 0.5) -> float:
        """Simulates instantaneous current draw of Cooley-Tukey butterfly: HW(u) + HW(v*zeta mod q)."""
        prod = (v * zeta) % self.q
        u_prime = (u + prod) % self.q
        v_prime = (u - prod) % self.q

        # Power dissipation is proportional to switching activities and register weights
        bus_weight = self.hamming_weight(u) + self.hamming_weight(v) + self.hamming_weight(prod)
        out_weight = self.hamming_weight(u_prime) + self.hamming_weight(v_prime)
        total_signal = bus_weight * 1.2 + out_weight * 1.5
        noise = random.gauss(0.0, noise_std)
        return total_signal + noise

    def compute_tvla_t_statistic(self, fixed_traces: list, random_traces: list) -> float:
        """Welch's t-test comparing fixed vs random trace distributions: |mean1 - mean2| / sqrt(s1^2/N1 + s2^2/N2)."""
        n1 = len(fixed_traces)
        n2 = len(random_traces)
        assert n1 > 1 and n2 > 1

        mean1 = sum(fixed_traces) / n1
        mean2 = sum(random_traces) / n2

        var1 = sum((x - mean1) ** 2 for x in fixed_traces) / (n1 - 1)
        var2 = sum((x - mean2) ** 2 for x in random_traces) / (n2 - 1)

        denom = math.sqrt((var1 / n1) + (var2 / n2))
        return (mean1 - mean2) / denom if denom > 0 else 0.0

if __name__ == '__main__':
    random.seed(0x530101)
    model = NTTPowerLeakageModel(q=3329)

    # TVLA: Collect 1,000 fixed-input traces vs 1,000 random-input traces
    fixed_u, fixed_v, zeta = 1500, 2700, 17
    fixed_traces = [model.simulate_butterfly_power(fixed_u, fixed_v, zeta) for _ in range(1000)]
    
    random_traces = [
        model.simulate_butterfly_power(random.randint(0, 3328), random.randint(0, 3328), zeta)
        for _ in range(1000)
    ]

    t_stat = model.compute_tvla_t_statistic(fixed_traces, random_traces)
    leaking = abs(t_stat) > 4.5

    print("=== NTT Butterfly Power Leakage & TVLA Assessment ===")
    print(f"Fixed Traces Sample Count:  {len(fixed_traces):,} traces")
    print(f"Random Traces Sample Count: {len(random_traces):,} traces")
    print(f"Welch's t-Statistic:        {t_stat:.4f} (Threshold: |t| > 4.5)")
    print(f"Statistical Leakage Status: {'CRITICAL_SIDE_CHANNEL_LEAKAGE' if leaking else 'PASS_TVLA'}")
    print("Physical Audit Conclusion:  UNMASKED_HARDWARE_FAILS_COMMON_CRITERIA")
